L1@P0: Historic Building Appraisal
L2@P0: Tin Hau Temple
L3@P0: Fong Ma Po, Lam Tsuen, Tai Po, N.T.
L4@P0:  Tin Hau Temple (天后宮) in Fong Ma Po (放馬莆), Lam Tsuen (林村/林村
L5@P0: 鄉), is believed to be built in the 33rd year of the Qianlong reign (乾隆,1768)
L6@P0: during the Qing (清) dynasty (1644 – 1911) as a cloud gong has the dating
L7@P0: inscribed on it. Fong Ma Po is one of the twenty-six villages in Lam Tsuen,
L8@P0: five of them are Punti (本地), whilst the others are Hakka (客家). In the Qing
L9@P0: dynasty the villages were divided into six units called kap (甲), each consisting
L10@P0: of about 100 households. The six kaps later formed an association called Luk
L11@P0: Wo Tong (六和堂, literally meaning hall of six harmonies) for the maintenance
L12@P0: of the temple. Its services then extended to other social and village affairs.
L13@P0: Fong Ma Po was founded in early Qing dynasty in the seventeenth century.
L14@P0: Being a Punti village, its main clans were the Wongs (黃) and Maks (麥). The
L15@P0: original name of the village was called Lung Hing Tsuen (龍興村) and later
L16@P0: renamed as Fong Ma Po, literally a place for horse grazing, when the villagers
L17@P0: started rearing horses in the area. The temple was destroyed by Typhoon Dot
L18@P0: (黛蒂) in 1964 and further damaged by a fire in 1965. It was then renovated
L19@P0: in 1967. It has three halls, the middle one being for Tin Hau, the left one
L20@P0: named Man Mo Court (文武殿) for Kwan Tai (關帝) with a tablet for twelve
L21@P0: martyrs who were said to have sacrificed for the defense of the village, and the
L22@P0: right one called Lung Mo Court (龍母殿) with a tablet of Tang Chim (鄧詹)
L23@P0: and his wife for their contribution in founding the temple. The temple is
L24@P0: managed by the local community.
L25@P0: Historical
L26@P0: Interest
L27@P0:  The temple is a Qing vernacular building on a
L28@P0: two-hall-one-courtyard-two-side-chamber plan with its roofs in flush gable
L29@P0: style (硬山). All three entrances are recessed. The granite columns,
L30@P0: grey-brick walls support the roofs which are with rafters, purlins and clay tiles.
L31@P0: The main ridge has a ceramic pearl, a pair of dragon fish locally known as
L32@P0: aoyus (鰲魚), plastered moulding of two fish and a set of geometric pattern.
L33@P0: Wall friezes and fascia boards are respectively with floral, plants, landscape and
L34@P0: scrolls carvings and paintings.
L35@P0: Architectural
L36@P0: Merit
L37@P0:  It is a Tin Hau temple to witness the historic development of Lam Tsuen.
L38@P0: The temple has moderate built heritage value. It was renovated in 1835, 1967
L39@P0: and 2001 with some other unknown ones. Plastering and the concrete
L40@P0: columns added have affected the authenticity of the historic building.
L41@P0: Rarity, Built
L42@P0: Heritage
L43@P0: Value &
L44@P0: Authenticity
L45@P0-1: 527
L46@P1:  Other than the Tin Hau Festival (天后誕) celebrated on the 23rd day of the
L47@P1: third lunar month, Ta Chiu (打醮) held every nine years in Lam Tsuen would
L48@P1: have great offerings at the temple with Cantonese opera performances,
L49@P1: vegetarian meals and others. The wishing trees (許願樹) by the temple have
L50@P1: attracted a lot of worshippers to both the trees and the temple especially during
L51@P1: the Chinese New Year.
L52@P1: Social Value,
L53@P1: & Local Interest
L54@P1:  There are no other graded historic buildings near the temple. Group Value
